newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Europe's big companies asked to help the small ones.
newsitem.headline: Europe's big companies asked to help the small ones.

text.p: Europe's ability to create jobs and compete on world markets would improve if big companies worked more closely with small ones, a report published by a group of top European corporations said on Monday.
The heavyweights should, for example, forge close business links with small companies, consider spinning off units to them and share training resources with them, it said.
"Partnerships between large and small companies have become a central feature of the business world," Morris Tabaksblat, chairman and CEO of Anglo-Dutch conglomerate Unilever Plc , said.

"Europe is losing out in comparison to its competitors," he told a luncheon of the European Round Table of Industrialists (ERT), which prepared the report. "It is not modernising its industrial and economic structures quickly enough."
The ERT groups the chairmen of 45 leading European companies.

The report found that small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) that received support from large companies had an 80 percent survival rate after five years -- compared with the 50 percent European average.
It highlighted the benefits of "positive restructuring", saying it entailed the cooperation of companies, employees and public authorities.

"Redundancy funds can be used imaginatively to help create sustainable new job opportunities," it said. "A dying unit of a large company can be replaced by healthy SMEs. Centres for new business activities can reinvigorate the surrounding community."
Governments could help by easing up on the regulatory burdens that hamper SMEs, "one of Europe's major competitive handicaps", it added.
The report also called for science parks and technology clusters bringing together large and small companies, university researchers, technical advisers and venture capitalists.
The ERT report is based on 40 case studies in areas ranging from commercial relationships to training and education.

It cited Swiss foods group Nestle SA, for example, for spinning off a printing unit that it acquired when it bought British confectionery company Rowntree -- to a major printing supplier in York, Lawson Mardon.
It offered to award all of Nestle's printing contracts to Lawson Mardon if it agreed to build a new printing plant in the city centre and to take in the former Rowntree's employees.

French oil company Total was cited for setting up a programme to help SMEs find export markets while Dutch electronics giant Philips was listed for setting up a work-experience project that sends workers to SMEs.
